d.title: Choosing a dtype on purpose
d.caption: The default is `float64` and it is rarely what you need. Halving the width halves the memory **and** doubles how much fits in cache, which is usually the larger win — but `float16` has about three decimal digits, so it is a storage format rather than a compute one.

d.title: View or copy, and how to tell
d.caption: The aliasing bug comes from not knowing which you have. The rule is mechanical: **basic** indexing can be expressed as a strided window, so it returns a view; **fancy** indexing cannot, so it copies. `arr.base` tells you after the fact.

d.title: Reductions and missing data
d.caption: A single NaN propagates through an ordinary reduction and makes the whole result NaN, which is correct and almost never what you want. The `nan*` family skips them — and then the divisor changes, which is the part that silently alters a mean.

cells.text: the COUNT of non-NaN — not n

d.title: What a seed can and cannot fix
d.caption: A seed makes one process reproducible. It does not survive threads, a different library version, or a dictionary iteration that was never ordered — so “I set the seed” is not the same claim as “this run reproduces”.
cells: deterministic kernels, and accept the cost

d.title: When an array stops being an array
d.caption: `object` dtype keeps the NumPy interface and loses everything that made it fast: the data is a block of **pointers**, so there is no contiguity, no vectorised loop and no fixed stride. It is a Python list wearing an array's clothes.

cells.text: a POINTER to a Python object

d.title: Growing an array in a loop
d.caption: `np.append` allocates a new array and copies everything every time, so building n elements costs O(n²) copies. A list appends in amortised O(1) and converts once at the end — the same total work a single allocation would have done.

d.title: Splitting, and what each one promises
d.caption: `split` insists the pieces come out equal and raises if they cannot; `array_split` quietly makes them uneven. Which you want depends on whether an uneven split is a bug or a fact of your data.
cells: as equal as it can manage

d.title: Set operations on arrays
d.caption: These all sort internally, so they are O(n log n) rather than the O(n) a hash set would give — but they return arrays and keep the dtype, which is usually what you want inside a vectorised pipeline. `in1d` is the one with a faster alternative.
cells: return_counts gives a frequency table free
in the first, not the second
order follows the sort, not the input

cells.text: the one you want for filtering

d.title: Never invert to solve
d.caption: `inv(A) @ b` computes something you did not need and loses accuracy doing it. `solve` factorises once and substitutes, which is both faster and better conditioned — and for a least-squares problem `lstsq` is better again, because it does not form AᵀA at all.

d.title: A structured array, or a DataFrame
d.caption: Structured arrays are row-major, so a whole-column operation touches every row's worth of bytes. That is the opposite of what analysis wants, and it is why pandas exists — a structured array is for a binary format with a fixed record layout.

columns.title: structured array
items: one block, records laid out row by row
a column operation strides over every record
no index, no alignment, no missing-value handling
right for reading a binary file with a fixed layout
right when you pass records to C

items: a column operation is a contiguous scan
an index, automatic alignment, a missing-value story

d.title: Every ufunc already has four methods
d.caption: These come free on any ufunc and replace a surprising amount of hand-written code. `at` is the one worth knowing: it does an **unbuffered** in-place update, so repeated indices accumulate instead of overwriting each other.

d.title: Finding a period with an FFT
d.caption: Four steps, and the third is where people go wrong: the x-axis of an FFT is frequency, so the period is its reciprocal, and the units follow your sample spacing rather than your intuition.

d.title: Alignment explains nearly every pandas surprise
d.caption: Arithmetic between two pandas objects matches on the **index**, not on position. Once that is held, the NaN that appeared from nowhere, the row count that grew after an operation, and the assignment that did nothing all have the same explanation.

items.desc: the union of both, so a label in only one side produces NaN

d.title: What a categorical buys beyond memory
d.caption: The memory saving is the advertised benefit and the smaller one. The real wins are that a groupby can use the codes directly, that an order can be declared and then sorted on, and that an unexpected value **raises** instead of being silently accepted.

cells.text: a declared order, so low < mid < high

d.title: Long and wide, and the verb for each direction
d.caption: Four functions and two directions. `pivot` raises on a duplicate index-column pair; `pivot_table` aggregates it instead — which is why a silent mean appears in results people did not ask for.

d.title: The five joins, by what each keeps
d.caption: The `how` argument decides which keys survive; the **cardinality** decides how many rows come back, and those are different questions. A many-to-many join can return more rows than either input — pass `validate=` and let pandas refuse.

cells.text: NaN where the right is missing

d.title: Duplicates: which copy survives
d.caption: `keep` is the argument that decides, and `keep=False` does not mean “keep none of the extras” — it means **drop every row that has a duplicate**, including the first. That difference quietly removes data.
